edition.deck: A deadly strike in Gaza, a blast at an Afghan school and fresh scrutiny of justice, security and public services.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting. Returning themes are included only where this gather offers a new development or useful current account; allegations and unverified claims remain attributed.

content.headline: Two MSF workers killed in Israeli strike on Gaza clinic, charity says
content.shortHeadline: MSF says two workers killed in Gaza clinic strike
content.standfirst: Médecins Sans Frontières says the clinic’s location was known to Israel’s military. The IDF says the men were Hamas operatives and that the strike was not directed at a hospital; the WHO condemned attacks on health workers.

image.caption: MSF says two of its workers were killed in the strike on the clinic.

sources.originalTitle: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says

segments.body: Two Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) workers were killed when an Israeli strike hit one of the charity’s clinics in Gaza, the organisation says. MSF says the site was clearly marked and its location had been shared with the Israeli military.

segments.title: Conflicting accounts
segments.body: The Israel Defense Forces says the two men were Hamas operatives acting as guards and that the strike was not directed at a hospital. The WHO condemned attacks on health workers and facilities. Witnesses told the BBC the men were at the clinic entrance when a drone fired.

content.headline: Afghanistan school blast kills at least 10 students, officials say
content.shortHeadline: Blast near Afghan school kills at least 10 students
content.standfirst: More than 100 people were injured in the explosion near a school in Kunar province. Taliban officials blame negligence at a nearby explosives depot, but say their investigation is still under way.

image.caption: A classroom was damaged in the explosion near the school in Asadabad.

sources.originalTitle: Afghanistan explosion kills 10 students and injures more than 100, official says

segments.body: At least 10 students were killed and 110 injured in an explosion near a school in Asadabad, the capital of Afghanistan’s Kunar province, an interior ministry spokesperson told the BBC. Officials say the blast happened on Saturday morning.

segments.title: Cause under investigation
segments.body: The ministry spokesperson said initial findings pointed to negligence at a nearby explosives depot belonging to mining companies. Another provincial official said explosives were being prepared at a house near the school. The investigation is ongoing; mining safety standards in Afghanistan are often poor, the BBC reports.

content.headline: China’s growing clout is making it harder for dissidents to be heard
content.shortHeadline: Exiled dissidents say China’s influence is silencing their cause
content.standfirst: Uyghur and Tibetan activists describe waning international attention and pressure surrounding family visits to China. Beijing rejects claims that it seeks information from exiles or tries to influence them.

image.caption: Uyghur and Tibetan activists say China’s growing influence is drawing attention away from their cause.

sources.originalTitle: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out

segments.body: Uyghur and Tibetan activists say China’s economic and diplomatic influence is making it harder to attract attention and support for their causes. Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa says rallies in Germany that once drew thousands now struggle to attract 500 people.

segments.title: Family ties and pressure
segments.body: Activists told the BBC that some exiles invited to visit relatives in China were asked for information about their networks or to promote pro-government messages. They say the visits can deepen fear and mistrust in exile communities. China’s embassy in the UK says family visits are a normal part of consular services and denies the allegations.

content.headline: Turkish authorities have ‘destroyed’ Halk TV, owner tells BBC
content.shortHeadline: Halk TV owner says arrests deepen Turkey’s media crackdown
content.standfirst: Nine people connected to the pro-opposition broadcaster have been arrested this week, its owner says. Prosecutors allege two former anchors produced paid-for false reports; the owner rejects the allegations.

image.caption: Halk TV owner Cafer Mahiroğlu says Turkish authorities have destroyed the broadcaster.

sources.originalTitle: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC

segments.body: Nine people connected to Halk TV have been arrested this week on allegations including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information, the channel’s London-based owner, Cafer Mahiroğlu, told the BBC. He says the claims against him and the broadcaster are “completely wrong”.

segments.title: Control of the channel
segments.body: Prosecutors say two former anchors were detained over alleged false reports produced in exchange for money. Authorities took control of Halk TV last month after a raid halted its broadcasts and appointed a new administrator. Mahiroğlu says the action is part of a wider effort to control the media; the government says it does not detain journalists for doing their work.

content.headline: Satellite study finds African coastal cities sinking faster than expected
content.shortHeadline: Satellite data finds faster sinking in Lagos and Alexandria
content.standfirst: Researchers say subsidence in some cities could increase flood exposure beyond earlier estimates. The study highlights both places where risks may be underestimated and areas where they may have been overstated.

image.caption: Researchers used satellite data to measure land movement in coastal cities including Lagos.

sources.originalTitle: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking

segments.body: Satellite measurements suggest that parts of Lagos and Alexandria are sinking faster than estimates made in 2021 by the UN climate science body, the IPCC. Researchers found average subsidence of about 5mm a year in Lagos and 6mm in Alexandria.

segments.title: Local causes, local choices
segments.body: Groundwater extraction, construction on loose ground and reclaimed land are among the possible causes identified in the study. Researchers estimate that by 2050, seven million people, one million buildings and $180bn in assets could face flood risk. They say the satellite method could help planners target local measures, from alternative water supplies to flood defences.

content.headline: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat after dispute over children’s camp
content.shortHeadline: North Korea orders Swiss diplomat out after camp sanctions
content.standfirst: The move came weeks after Switzerland reopened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and joined EU sanctions targeting a North Korean children’s camp. Allegations that Ukrainian children were sent there for indoctrination remain difficult to verify.

image.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un is shown at the Songdowon children’s camp in 2014.

sources.originalTitle: En børnelejr i Nordkorea har udløst et diplomatisk opgør med Schweiz

segments.body: North Korea has ordered Switzerland’s diplomat in Pyongyang to leave within 48 hours and close the diplomatic office, which reopened less than a month ago. Switzerland had joined EU sanctions targeting an international children’s camp in the North Korean port city of Wonsan.

segments.title: Allegations and consequences
segments.body: Ukrainian media have reported that children from Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine attended the camp; a Danish defence analyst cited in the report says the visits may be part of Russian indoctrination. Details from inside North Korea are scarce, and Kim Yo-jong condemned the sanctions without directly addressing the allegations. Switzerland says relations will continue through its embassies in Beijing and Bern.

content.headline: Hundreds of thousands remain without power after US holiday storms
content.shortHeadline: More than 260,000 still without power after US storms
content.standfirst: Severe weather brought flooding, high winds and widespread travel disruption over Thanksgiving. Power cuts were easing by Friday evening, but forecasters warned another storm could bring heavy rain and strong winds next week.

image.caption: Thanksgiving storms flooded roads and brought down trees in parts of the United States.

sources.originalTitle: Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms

segments.body: More than 260,000 people in the United States remained without power on Friday evening after storms hit both coasts during the Thanksgiving holiday. The number of reported outages had peaked at nearly a million on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania among the hardest-hit states.

segments.title: Travel and weather ahead
segments.body: Flooding, closed roads and flight disruption affected holiday travel. More than 3,400 flights were delayed and nearly 670 cancelled on Friday, according to the report. Conditions were expected to improve in the north-east, but another area of low pressure could bring heavy rain and strong winds on Monday.

content.headline: Ukraine says laser weapon shot down Russian drone in combat first
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says combat laser brought down a Russian drone
content.standfirst: A Ukrainian presidential adviser says the system was used to defend critical infrastructure. Experts describe the technology as promising but unproven at scale, with weather and electricity supply limiting its use.

image.caption: Drones have become a critical weapon for both Russia and Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: The Star Wars-style weapon designed to keep Ukrainians safe from drones

segments.body: Ukraine says a laser-based system called Blysk shot down a Russian jet-powered Geran drone during an attack on critical infrastructure. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, called it the first use of a laser weapon in combat against Russia. The system’s performance has not been independently established in the reporting.

segments.title: Limits remain
segments.body: Beskrestnov says it is too early to discuss mass production. Security expert Jane Hardy says the demonstration is significant but doubts it will change the war’s immediate course. Rain, fog and cloud can weaken a laser beam, while repeated Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid may constrain how many systems can operate.

content.headline: UN maritime tribunal rejects Argentina’s bid to halt Falklands oil project
content.shortHeadline: Argentina fails to stop Falklands oil project at UN tribunal
content.standfirst: The tribunal said it lacked jurisdiction to decide a sovereignty dispute. Argentina says the ruling does not legitimise drilling and has announced sanctions against five entities; the project’s developers welcomed the decision.

image.caption: Port Stanley in the Falkland Islands, where residents voted in 2013 to remain a British overseas territory.

sources.originalTitle: Argentina fails to block oil drilling off Falkland Islands
Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected
FN-domstol afviser at stoppe britisk-israelsk olieprojekt ved Falklandsøerne

segments.body: An international maritime tribunal has rejected Argentina’s request to suspend the Sea Lion oil project near the Falkland Islands, saying it could not rule on sovereignty. Eighteen judges voted against the request and three supported it. The UK says the ruling backs the islanders’ right to determine their future.

segments.title: Dispute continues
segments.body: Argentina says it did not ask the tribunal to rule on sovereignty and maintains that the drilling is an unlawful exploitation of its resources. Its government says it has begun sanction proceedings against five entities, without naming them. The project’s developers, Navitas and Rockhopper, plan to begin drilling in March, with extraction expected from 2028.

content.headline: Guardian finds most US airmen convicted of child abuse in UK faced courts-mart-m
content.shortHeadline: Most US airmen convicted of child abuse in UK faced US courts
content.standfirst: The Guardian identified 21 cases over the past decade and found only three were prosecuted in UK courts. The report raises questions about transparency and how an agreement between the two countries is applied.

image.caption: US military personnel work at more than a dozen bases and facilities across the UK.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Please can I have one more picture’: the US airmen accused of child sexual abuse in UK who avoided British trial

segments.body: A Guardian investigation identified at least 21 US airmen in Britain convicted of child sexual abuse offences in the past decade. Only three were prosecuted in UK courts; the others faced US military courts-martial held on US bases. The report says records of those proceedings are often difficult for the public to access.

segments.title: Jurisdiction and scrutiny
segments.body: An agreement dating to the 1950s says UK police should investigate US personnel accused of offences, except in specified circumstances. The Guardian says UK forces have sometimes agreed to US requests to take over cases, and that a high-level inquiry is examining whether prosecutions are being handled properly. The US Air Force says jurisdiction is determined with UK partners and local authorities have the right of first refusal.

content.headline: Police make 33 arrests in Southampton child sexual abuse inquiry
content.shortHeadline: 33 arrested as Southampton police investigate sexual abuse claims
content.standfirst: Hampshire police say they have seized more than 80 phones as they investigate concerns about men in contact with teenage girls. Two men face separate court proceedings; the wider inquiry is continuing.

image.caption: Hampshire police say their inquiry includes concerns about men in contact with teenage girls.

sources.originalTitle: Police make 33 arrests as part of child sexual abuse inquiry in Southampton

segments.body: Police investigating allegations of sexual abuse involving teenage girls in Southampton say they have arrested 33 people and seized more than 80 mobile phones. The force says it is reviewing material and has placed strict bail conditions on those arrested.

segments.title: Separate cases
segments.body: Sayeed Hashimi, 22, has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old and is due to be sentenced in January. Aster Simon, 35, is charged with offences including rape and sexual assault involving a 15-year-old; he is due to stand trial next month. The allegations against Simon have not been determined in court.

content.headline: Judges told to warn juries against rape myths in sexual offence trials
content.shortHeadline: New guidance says judges should always address rape myths
content.standfirst: Updated guidance for judges in England and Wales says warnings about misconceptions surrounding sexual violence should always be given. The change follows criticism of the defence in Russell Brand’s trial.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at court during his trial.

sources.originalTitle: Judges ‘should always’ tell jurors to disregard rape myths, new guidance for England and Wales says

segments.body: Judges in England and Wales have been told that directions warning juries against rape myths “should always be given”. The Crown Court Compendium says the guidance is important even when lawyers do not explicitly rely on stereotypes about how people respond to sexual assault.

segments.title: Different responses
segments.body: The guidance says people react differently to serious sexual assault and that a delayed report does not automatically make a complaint unreliable. A senior Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor said there is no single “right way” to respond to sexual abuse. The update follows criticism of questions put to complainants during Russell Brand’s trial.

content.headline: Experts warn AI breakthroughs could unsettle encryption, but evidence is unclear
content.shortHeadline: AI encryption fears grow, but experts say no breakthrough is confirmed
content.standfirst: Computer scientists cite unverified reports and recent mathematical advances as reasons to prepare for possible changes to cryptography. No AI company has announced a discovery that breaks widely used encryption.

image.caption: Encryption protects sensitive communications such as banking transactions, diplomatic messages and private email.

sources.originalTitle: AI labs sitting on ‘bombshell’ revelations that could cause global chaos, experts believe
Could AI break encryption? What mathematical breakthroughs mean for cybersecurity

segments.body: Computer scientists say recent AI advances in mathematics have raised questions about whether models might find new ways to break encryption. Scott Aaronson told the Guardian he had heard “well-attested rumours” of possible breakthroughs, but no AI company has announced such a discovery and the reporting does not establish that encryption has been broken.

segments.title: Verification and preparation
segments.body: Experts quoted by the Guardian say the implications are uncertain: a discovery might expose some secrets, or show that information is more secure than expected. Mathematical proofs attributed to AI still need human verification. Governments and companies are already preparing for quantum-era risks, but some experts say organisations reliant on encryption should be ready to respond more quickly.

content.headline: Barrister describes racist abuse after MP shares ceremony photo
content.shortHeadline: Barrister says MP’s viral post triggered racist abuse online
content.standfirst: Joseph Ashong says a photograph of newly qualified barristers was circulated as supposed evidence of discrimination against white Britons. The post drew millions of views and was followed by racist abuse, according to the Guardian investigation.

image.caption: Joseph Ashong, seventh from left, at his call-to-the-bar ceremony.

sources.originalTitle: Black barrister tells of racist abuse after Rupert Lowe viral tweet

segments.body: Joseph Ashong, a newly qualified barrister, says he was shocked by racist abuse after Rupert Lowe shared a group photograph from a call-to-the-bar ceremony, presenting it as evidence of discrimination against white Britons. The post was viewed 2.3 million times, the Guardian reports.

segments.title: Reaction and representation
segments.body: Ashong, who came to the UK from Ghana and received a Middle Temple scholarship, says the suggestion that the photograph showed bias was “ignorant”. A second barrister pictured in another post also described the reaction as abuse. A Restore Britain spokesperson said Lowe’s post spoke for itself; the report notes that most barristers in England and Wales are white.

content.headline: Overseas-trained doctors say UK training priority has closed career routes
content.shortHeadline: Overseas-trained doctors describe impact of UK training priority law
content.standfirst: A 2026 law gives UK medical graduates and other eligible groups priority for specialty training. Overseas-trained doctors interviewed by the i Paper say the change has narrowed their options; ministers say it protects opportunities for UK-trained doctors.

image.caption: Eftychia Kiousi moved to Britain hoping to train as a paediatrician.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a foreign-born doctor – my dream of living in the UK is over because of a new law

segments.body: A law introduced in March gives UK medical graduates and other eligible groups priority for specialty training places. The i Paper reports that the share of accepted offers going to doctors outside the priority group fell from 28% in 2025 to 1.8% in 2026, according to provisional NHS England figures analysed by the Nuffield Trust.

segments.title: Different paths, different views
segments.body: Two overseas-trained doctors told the i Paper that the change has weakened their plans to train in the UK; one is preparing to return to Greece and another is seeking a position nearer home. A third, who asked not to be identified, said he had left the UK after his contract was not renewed, but the report does not establish that this was caused by the law. The Government says prioritisation protects investment in UK training; the BMA supports it while also calling for better progression for international graduates.

content.headline: Burnham’s 10-year plan faces questions over ambition and delivery
content.shortHeadline: Burnham’s long-term plan draws hopes and doubts inside Labour
content.standfirst: The Prime Minister is expected to publish a national blueprint by 17 December, covering areas including energy, welfare and regional powers. Labour MPs and policy commentators question whether it can be detailed, coherent and deliverable.

image.caption: Andy Burnham is due to set out the government’s long-term plan.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Andy holds the pen’: will Burnham’s 10-year plan live up to the hype?

segments.body: Andy Burnham is expected to publish a 10-year plan for the UK by 17 December. Downing Street says he will write it, with ideas being developed on energy, welfare, European relations, a national care service and devolving powers to regions.

segments.title: Pressure to deliver
segments.body: Some Labour MPs worry the plan may be too vague or insufficiently ambitious, while policy commentator Neal Lawson says the process risks being too technocratic and top-down. Others argue a clear account of how existing policies fit together would be useful. Officials’ ability to complete the work on time remains uncertain.

content.headline: More people join Denmark’s Home Guard as security concerns grow
content.shortHeadline: Home Guard recruitment remains high amid security concerns
content.standfirst: More than 1,700 people joined in the first ten months of the year, following a record increase last year. New recruit Mathilde Kromann Petersen says she wants to show the force does more than direct traffic.

image.caption: New Home Guard volunteer Mathilde Kromann Petersen says she is looking forward to joining the force.

sources.originalTitle: Mathilde er ny i Hjemmeværnet: ’Det handler ikke kun om at dirigere trafik’

segments.body: Denmark’s Home Guard says 1,710 people joined in the first ten months of 2026. That is slightly fewer than in the same period last year, when recruitment recorded its strongest growth in four decades, but markedly more than in 2024. The force has just under 16,000 active members.

segments.title: A new recruit
segments.body: Mathilde Kromann Petersen, 29, decided to join after meeting volunteers during an exercise at Aalborg harbour. She says she wants to help present the Home Guard as a professional force with a role beyond directing traffic. The regional recruitment chief says people are motivated by a wish to help protect Denmark.

content.headline: Denmark moves to bar prosecutors from wearing religious symbols in court
content.shortHeadline: New neutrality rules would bar prosecutors’ religious symbols
content.standfirst: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked the director of public prosecutions to issue guidelines requiring prosecutors to appear religiously and politically neutral in court. Prosecutor Zahra Sediqi says the change could force her to change duties or remove her headscarf.

sources.originalTitle: Her er Zahra. Hun kan ikke længere være anklager i retten

segments.body: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked the director of public prosecutions to introduce guidelines barring prosecutors from wearing religious or political symbols in court. The ministry says prosecutors should appear neutral, as judges are required to do under existing law.

segments.title: A prosecutor’s objection
segments.body: Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor who wears a headscarf, says the change restricts women’s opportunities on the basis of religion and does not make a person impartial. Wammen says prosecutors will need to leave religious headwear at home when appearing in court. The rules are to be introduced as internal guidelines, not an extension of the statute governing judges.

content.headline: Dead pigs left exposed at Danish farm, inspection report says
content.shortHeadline: Six dead pigs found exposed at farm, Danish report says
content.standfirst: A Danish inspection found six pig carcasses outside a Holbæk farm and cats feeding on one of them. The farm’s owner says procedures are followed; a later inspection recorded no problems with storage of dead animals.

image.caption: Footage from a veterinary inspection shows cats near dead pigs at the Holbæk property.

sources.originalTitle: Flere overtrædelser: Styrelse fandt halvspiste svinekadavere uden for svinegigants stald

segments.body: A Danish Veterinary and Food Administration inspection found six dead pigs outside a farm in Holbæk municipality in August. Its report says two cats were seen feeding on one carcass and two were visibly gnawed. The farm was told to ensure dead animals were stored under cover until collection.

segments.title: Health concerns and response
segments.body: A veterinary virologist told DR that carcasses accessible to animals can create a risk of disease spreading to livestock and, in some circumstances, people. The farmer, Peter Kjær Knudsen, says staff move dead pigs to a collection point and that a later inspection found no problems with storage. He did not address DR’s questions about cat faeces found in grain; the inspection also ordered the grain destroyed.

content.headline: Denmark to refund some disputed state debts after long delays
content.shortHeadline: State to repay some disputed debts, including interest
content.standfirst: The government expects to return about 26 million kroner after problems with the debt-collection system left some payments in doubt. Small claims will be written off; larger ones will be reviewed manually during 2027.

image.caption: Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt says people and businesses have waited too long for clarity.

sources.originalTitle: Staten skal betale ugyldig gæld tilbage til folk

segments.body: The Danish state expects to repay about 26 million kroner, including interest, to people and businesses who may have paid debts that were not valid. The uncertainty followed the 2015 collapse of the tax authority’s debt-collection system. Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt says people have waited too long for clarity.

segments.title: How the review works
segments.body: Debts of up to 5,000 kroner will be cancelled, and people who already paid them will receive refunds with interest. Larger claims will be reviewed manually during 2027; if a debt is found not to have been owed, it will also be repaid with interest. Minimum refund thresholds apply, including separate thresholds for estates and bankruptcies.

content.headline: Teenager denies murder after fatal stabbing in Gentofte
content.shortHeadline: 19-year-old denies murder after fatal Gentofte stabbing
content.standfirst: A 19-year-old has been remanded in custody for four weeks after a 21-year-old died from multiple stab wounds. The accused says he acted in self-defence; key details remain under investigation.

image.caption: Police worked at Fuglegårdsvænget in Gentofte, where the stabbing took place.

sources.originalTitle: Stak offer flere gange: 19-årig nægter sig skyldig i drab

segments.body: A 21-year-old man has died after being stabbed several times in Gentofte on Friday evening. A 19-year-old, charged with murder, denies the accusation and says he acted in self-defence, according to his lawyer at a remand hearing.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The 19-year-old has been remanded for four weeks. The hearing was held behind closed doors and a name publication ban is in place. Police have not established whether the two men knew each other or whether anyone else was involved; they say there is no indication the killing was gang-related.

content.headline: Danish food agency recalls baked goods after contaminated grain case
content.shortHeadline: More Danish foods recalled after contaminated grain case
content.standfirst: Flour, apple dumplings and Christmas biscuits are among products recalled over elevated mycotoxins. Authorities say there is no acute health impact from eating the affected food, but a longer-term risk cannot be ruled out.

image.caption: Several flour and baked-goods products have been recalled in Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: Tilbagekaldelse på tilbagekaldelse: Kan du spise småkager med ro i maven?

segments.body: Denmark’s food authority has recalled several products, including flour, apple dumplings and Christmas biscuits, after a case involving grain declared unfit for human consumption. The affected products were made with flour containing elevated levels of mycotoxins, toxins produced by mould.

segments.title: What consumers can do
segments.body: The authority says there is no acute health effect from eating the affected foods, but it cannot rule out risk from longer-term exposure. Many recalled products may already be past their best-before dates. Consumers are advised to check the authority’s online list for affected products and dates; it remains unclear whether more recalls will follow.

content.headline: Danish charity shops say rejected donations cost millions to dispose of
content.shortHeadline: Unusable donations cost Danish charity shops millions to discard
content.standfirst: Charities say unsellable goods left at their shops bring substantial disposal costs and take volunteers away from other work. The ministry says an EU “polluter pays” principle prevents a general exemption from waste fees.

image.caption: Unsellable donations at a Kirkens Korshær shop must be taken to a waste facility.

sources.originalTitle: Tonsvis af affald stilles foran genbrugsbutikkerne: Regningen løber op i millioner
De her ting behøver du ikke give til genbrug - det bliver alligevel smidt ud

segments.body: Danish charity shops say discarded donations, including broken toys and unusable furniture, cost them millions of kroner to dispose of. Kirkens Korshær says it spends more than two million kroner a year on waste fees; the Salvation Army says its fees will exceed 600,000 kroner in 2026.

segments.title: Who pays?
segments.body: The Climate, Energy and Utilities Ministry says exempting the shops would conflict with the EU principle that the polluter pays. ISOBRO, the charities’ industry association, argues it is unfair for shops to pay to dispose of items residents have already paid to discard through municipal fees. A law due in 2028 will remove fees for textile waste, prompting calls to extend the change to other donations.

content.headline: Danish researchers test AI tool that estimates death risk from a face
content.shortHeadline: AI face-analysis tool shows promise but needs more testing
content.standfirst: A study using nearly 28,000 emergency-department patient photos found its model outperformed a current risk score at predicting early death. The researchers say it is not in use in hospitals and needs further testing.

image.caption: An illustration depicts the facial features analysed by the researchers’ AI model.

sources.originalTitle: AI kan forudsige dødsrisiko ud fra et enkelt billede

segments.body: Researchers from the University of Copenhagen and other institutions developed an AI model that estimates a patient’s risk of death from a facial photograph. In a study using nearly 28,000 images of patients at Herlev Hospital, the model was 34% better than the early warning score used in emergency departments at predicting premature death.

segments.title: Not ready for clinical use
segments.body: The researchers say the model is not being used in emergency departments and needs further testing; it could be years before it is ready to support clinical decisions. They hope it might eventually flag patients whose risk is not apparent from current measures. The study’s reported results do not establish how the tool would perform in other hospitals or populations.

content.headline: How Sleater-Kinney’s ‘Call the Doctor’ helped one listener leave a controlling
content.shortHeadline: The Sleater-Kinney song that helped her leave
content.standfirst: A writer recalls how the band’s forceful second album gave her a language for a relationship she had not yet recognised as controlling—and the resolve to end it.

image.caption: Illustration accompanying the writer’s account of discovering Sleater-Kinney’s Call the Doctor.

sources.originalTitle: A riot grrrl song inspired me to leave a controlling relationship

segments.body: As a teenager in the 1990s, the writer was encouraged by her boyfriend to play guitar, until he began insisting that it was his territory and demanding she give it up. Isolated and unsure how to describe his jealousy and control, she found a moment of recognition in Sleater-Kinney’s “Call the Doctor.”

segments.title: A song becomes a way out
segments.body: The record’s jagged guitars and Corin Tucker’s declaration, “We’re s’posed to be free / I’m s’posed to be mine,” helped the writer see a different possibility. She describes putting the album on during a difficult phone call and ending the relationship. Later, she joined a peer-training group to help other teenagers recognise controlling and abusive behaviour.

Thirty years after its release, she still hears the album as urgent, and as a door opening for her own life. Her account connects a particular record’s raw force to the practical importance of recognising abuse and finding support.

content.headline: Judee Sill’s brilliant songs are finding a new audience decades after her death
content.shortHeadline: Judee Sill’s music finds new listeners
content.standfirst: The singer-songwriter’s two albums won acclaim but not lasting commercial success. Renewed attention, including a documentary and the release of final recordings, is bringing her music to listeners who may wonder how it was overlooked.

image.caption: Judee Sill in London in 1972.

sources.originalTitle: The forgotten folk genius who’s finally getting her due after dying in obscurity

segments.body: Judee Sill’s musical life held stark contrasts: serene, intricate songs alongside years marked by addiction, homelessness and violence. Though she shared stages and a label with major artists, her career stalled after two albums, and she died at 35 in 1979. The source says her death was ruled a suicide, while noting that some believe the note found near her body was a plea for help.

segments.title: A catalogue worth rediscovering
segments.body: Sill wrote, arranged and produced her second album, Heart Food, which includes “The Kiss”; her self-titled debut brought together folk, country, gospel and baroque influences. The source points to later artists covering her songs, the documentary Lost Angel and Jim O’Rourke’s release of her final recordings as reasons her work is reaching new listeners.

content.headline: KLF-backed People’s Pyramid turns grief into a communal day of remembrance
content.shortHeadline: Birkenhead’s People’s Pyramid makes grief communal
content.standfirst: In Birkenhead, relatives and volunteers add bricks containing cremated remains to a growing monument. The annual event mixes ritual, noise and celebration as families remember the dead together.

image.caption: Participants begin the procession at Birkenhead’s Day of the Dead.

sources.originalTitle: ‘My brother was its first body’: would you add your corpse to Birkenhead’s pyramid of dead people?

segments.body: The People’s Pyramid is being built from 34,592 bricks, each incorporating a small portion of a person’s cremated remains. At this year’s Birkenhead Day of the Dead, 39 people are added, bringing the total to 159. The project was announced by Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond of the KLF, but its organisers say it has become its own community event.

segments.title: A ritual made together
segments.body: Participants take on roles in a day that moves from a procession and offerings to a quiet brick-laying ceremony, followed by a minute of shouting the names of the dead. Families describe meeting each year as an anchor for remembrance; for some, the project offers a more personal tribute than a conventional funeral or scattering of ashes.

segments.title: Beyond its origin story
segments.body: The pyramid is currently kept in a shipping container and taken out for the ceremony. Organisers hope to find a permanent home for it in Birkenhead Park, but say they lose money running the event. Cauty says the KLF connection should recede as the project develops.

content.headline: La Ola Nocturna uncovers a restless, inventive Spanish pop underground
content.shortHeadline: The Spanish ’80s pop underground, rediscovered
content.standfirst: This third compilation of Spain’s 1980s pop vanguard moves from post-punk to synth-pop, revisiting artists who made music amid a burst of creativity after Franco’s death.

sources.originalTitle: La Ola Nocturna: Experimental Songs & Deviant Pop From the Spanish ’80s

segments.body: La Ola Nocturna gathers music associated with La Movida Madrileña and other strands of Spain’s 1980s underground. The review hears a wide-ranging compilation—playful, abrasive, sweet and strange—and praises its focus on an era and scene that have received less attention than earlier Spanish music retrospectives.

segments.title: A scene in many forms
segments.body: The selection ranges from Aventuras de Kirlian’s spare “En Invierno” to the dance-pop of Esclarecidos and the tougher “The Girl Is Mine” by Kremlyn. The review also notes how limited resources shaped the scene: for many artists, cassettes were the format available, if their music was released at all.

The reviewer connects the compilation’s sounds to contemporary Spanish and Spanish-speaking artists, hearing a continuing conversation rather than a closed historical chapter. The collection makes a case for giving this neglected music a more secure place in the canon.

content.headline: Font’s ‘American Bully XL’ lets tenderness emerge through distortion
content.shortHeadline: Font find vulnerability in the noise
content.standfirst: The Texas band turns from the cryptic post-punk of its debut towards more exposed songwriting, using harsh electronics and country inflections to frame songs of heartbreak and longing.

sources.originalTitle: American Bully XL

segments.body: On American Bully XL, Font shift towards more direct emotional territory. Thom Waddill’s lyrics centre on heartbreak and the desire to be understood, while industrial distortion, synths and dense percussion often make his voice sound strained or almost submerged.

segments.title: Country feeling, refracted
segments.body: The review finds the band’s country influences most compelling when they are warped by the production: a fragmentary ballad feeling in “Bad Faith,” and synths that move between the acoustic and the artificial on “Texas.” That tension lets vulnerability come through the noise rather than simply soften it.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s solo debut brings traditional songs into a vivid new present
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat makes old songs feel newly alive
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer’s first solo album centres on her resonant voice, setting traditional songs and complicated female characters against arrangements that move between folk, keyboards and trip-hop.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: No Human Tongue Can Tell puts Radie Peat’s voice at its centre. She plays nearly every instrument and layers her own vocals, drawing material from Irish, British and American song traditions. The review hears a collection linked by its attention to women whose choices are constrained or whose stories are rarely heard.

segments.title: Tradition, rearranged
segments.body: Peat places songs about abuse, loss and agency in conversation across time, while changing their musical shape. “Hares on the Mountain” is recast with vintage keyboards, and “The Moon and Stars” turns a fiddle tune into a trip-hop-inflected piece that builds towards a crashing finish.

The review’s central pleasure is the contrast between Peat’s old-sounding, commanding voice and arrangements that can feel startlingly contemporary. The songs retain their roots even as the album makes them feel newly present.

content.headline: Thoom fuses Arabic instrumentation and hyperpop on a debut about belonging
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop personal and expansive
content.standfirst: Zeynab Marwan’s debut pairs hyperpop production with Arabic instruments and pop drama. Its most affecting moment turns a breakup song into a question about whether she can return to Lebanon.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, Los Angeles-based artist Zeynab Marwan, who performs as Thoom, brings Arabic instrumentation into hyperpop’s bright, fractured production. The review highlights her voice as the album’s anchor, moving from melodic phrasing to an edge of threat and anger.

segments.title: The personal and the political
segments.body: The songs range from the pounding “Janani” to the quieter “Morocco,” but the closing “I’m Going Back to Lebanon” gives the album its clearest statement of longing. Its questions about home and the possibility of return leave the song open to the uncertainty of the country’s continuing crisis.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s ‘Back to Black’ remains a landmark breakup album
content.shortHeadline: Why Back to Black still holds together
content.standfirst: A 20th-anniversary edition adds a handful of previously unheard recordings to Winehouse’s acclaimed 2006 album. The review considers what the extras reveal—and what no reissue can recover.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Back to Black turns the end of Amy Winehouse’s relationship with Blake Fielder-Civil into a tightly shaped song cycle, moving from the early intimacy of “Just Friends” to the title track’s desolation and the self-reliance of “Tears Dry on Their Own.” The anniversary edition includes early versions that show how the record developed.

segments.title: What the extras can—and cannot—add
segments.body: The review praises Winehouse’s range and the album’s fusion of older soul and girl-group sounds with modern language and attitude. It also finds the new material limited: five previously unheard tracks and a small number of demos sit alongside recordings already available elsewhere. The planned follow-up’s demos were destroyed, leaving a gap no expanded edition can fill.

content.headline: Wild Horse Nine brings Chile’s dictatorship into the cinema—and its streets
content.shortHeadline: Wild Horse Nine, haunted by Chile’s past
content.standfirst: A Chilean writer and survivor of the 1973 coup reflects on watching Martin McDonagh’s film in Santiago, near sites of torture and disappearance, and asks what younger viewers know of that history.

image.caption: Mariana di Girolamo and John Malkovich in Wild Horse Nine.

sources.originalTitle: Watching Wild Horse Nine in Santiago brings Pinochet’s tyranny back to dreadful life

segments.body: For the writer, watching Wild Horse Nine in Santiago was inseparable from having survived the coup that led to Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship. The film follows CIA agents whose actions help destroy Salvador Allende’s government and foreshadows the violence that follows, including the fate awaiting its fictional student, Mónica.

segments.title: A city marked by memory
segments.body: The cinema stands near places connected to people the writer knew: Diana Arón, a pregnant former student who disappeared, and Carmen Bueno, an actor who was raped and murdered in detention. The writer describes a brief conversation with younger audience members who did not recognise nearby sites or victims’ names, while acknowledging that a small, anecdotal encounter cannot stand for a whole generation.

The film also recalls US interventions in other countries, a dimension that resonates with the writer as both a Chilean and a US citizen. They hope the story can contribute to efforts to resist forgetting and to face the consequences of political violence.

content.headline: This week’s cinema releases range from political noir to a killer unicorn
content.shortHeadline: This week’s cinema: noir, family drama and a killer unicorn
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s critics weigh up new films including Andrey Zvyagintsev’s wartime Russian thriller, David Fincher’s return to Cliff Booth and Disney animation Hexed, alongside a slate of dramas and documentaries.

image.caption: Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro in Focker-in-Law.

sources.originalTitle: Hot or not? The Guardian’s film critics run the rule over the week’s UK cinema releases

segments.body: The week’s releases span crime, family drama, documentary and horror. The roundup includes Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, a noir set in wartime Russia; a coming-of-age story about a teenager’s online deception; and David Fincher’s continuation of Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, with Brad Pitt back as stuntman Cliff Booth.

segments.title: A mixed verdict on familiar worlds
segments.body: The selection also takes in Ava DuVernay’s defence of democracy, a documentary about Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty, a Korean family mystery and a film about Gaza refugees drawing their former neighbourhoods. The critics are less convinced by Disney’s Hexed, Focker-in-Law and a horror comedy built around a murderous TV-show unicorn.

content.headline: Netflix’s Christmas films turn familiar clichés into a festive tradition
content.shortHeadline: Why Netflix’s Christmas films keep finding an audience
content.standfirst: The streamer’s seasonal romances may be knowingly formulaic, but stars and makers say their promise of comfort and escape is part of the appeal. Their popularity has made these films a holiday ritual in their own right.

image.caption: Maddie Ziegler and Graham Phillips in In a Holidaze.

sources.originalTitle: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas

segments.body: Netflix’s Christmas films lean on familiar ingredients: romance, family reunions and low-stakes problems resolved in time for the holiday. The feature looks at how the streamer’s originals, from A Christmas Prince onward, became a recurring seasonal offering alongside the much larger Hallmark slate.

segments.title: The appeal of a safe landing
segments.body: Actors Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid, along with writers and filmmakers, describe the films as a chance to escape into stories where things turn out well. Netflix figures cited in the feature show holiday titles regularly appearing in the UK weekly top 10, despite their frequently lukewarm critical reception.

The feature sets that comfort against questions about streaming services’ preference for familiar, broadly appealing content over riskier projects. It suggests the formula’s very predictability may be part of the point for viewers seeking warmth and reassurance.

content.headline: December’s film calendar pairs Marvel spectacle with intimate dramas
content.shortHeadline: The films to look out for this December
content.standfirst: From Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three to Ava DuVernay’s 14th and Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care, this viewing guide ranges across cinema and streaming releases for the month ahead.

sources.originalTitle: Avengers: Doomsday to The Debut: 12 of the best films to watch this December

segments.body: The December selection covers blockbusters, animation, documentary and independent drama. Its largest event is Avengers: Doomsday, which brings together characters from several Marvel universes, while Dune: Part Three continues Denis Villeneuve’s adaptation of Frank Herbert’s novels.

segments.title: Beyond the big releases
segments.body: Other picks include Ava DuVernay’s documentary 14th, Tender Loving Care—described as Mike Leigh’s likely final film—and The Debut, starring Julianne Moore. The guide also points to the animated noir Ray Gunn, the historical drama Rose and an adaptation of Mrs Dalloway relocated to contemporary Lagos.

content.headline: The Hunting Wives uses sex and scandal to play with America’s political divide
content.shortHeadline: The Hunting Wives makes the culture war a soap
content.standfirst: The Netflix series returns to its wealthy East Texas community of secrets, affairs and political performance. Its appeal, the feature argues, lies in skewering both sides without losing the pleasures of glossy soap.

sources.originalTitle: 'It appeals across demographics': How steamy soap The Hunting Wives took on sex, scandal and the US's blue-red divide

segments.body: The Hunting Wives centres on Sophie, a liberal newcomer, and Margo, the wife of a conservative Texas political hopeful. Their affair unfolds amid murder, social manoeuvring and culture-war tensions. The show’s second season leans further into its eroticism, while a third has already been confirmed.

segments.title: Politics as performance
segments.body: The feature’s interviewees describe a series that mocks both Republican and Democrat characters, often treating politics as a cynical performance rather than taking a position on partisan disputes. A Texas journalist also argues that the show’s clashes reflect the state’s varied political life, where people with opposing views regularly meet.

The series’ emphasis on female pleasure is another part of its identity. Malin Åkerman credits its female creator, showrunner and directors with shaping scenes around what women find attractive, rather than simply reproducing familiar television conventions.

content.headline: Chicken Shop Date ends its 12-year run with an unexpectedly candid goodbye
content.shortHeadline: Amelia Dimoldenberg says goodbye to Chicken Shop Date
content.standfirst: The YouTube interview series closes with a conversation that turns into a therapy session, as Dimoldenberg reflects on outgrowing the show that made her famous and what she wants to do next.

image.caption: Amelia Dimoldenberg with Esther Perel.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Genuinely emotional’: the world-conquering Chicken Shop Date’s final, eye-opening episode

segments.body: After 12 years of awkward flirtation and celebrity interviews, Amelia Dimoldenberg’s final Chicken Shop Date episode features psychotherapist Esther Perel. The review finds a striking departure from the show’s familiar persona: Dimoldenberg speaks openly about the sadness and exhaustion of continuing a format she has outgrown.

segments.title: A goodbye to the show itself
segments.body: Prompted to imagine speaking directly to Chicken Shop Date, Dimoldenberg thanks the series and describes what she would lose by carrying on. She becomes tearful. The review places that farewell in the context of the show’s gradual rise—from a youth-club idea and early musician interviews to viral moments and an appearance at the Oscars.

The final series was screened in cinemas before its YouTube finale, a choice the reviewer initially questions but ultimately sees as a lap of honour. Dimoldenberg is now writing a romantic comedy and hopes to direct films.

content.headline: The Witch Farm brings Danny Robins’s uncertain ghost stories to television
content.shortHeadline: Danny Robins keeps the mysteries open
content.standfirst: The Uncanny host discusses adapting his podcast about a Welsh haunting, his fear of death and why he prefers stories that leave room for both belief and scepticism.

image.caption: Danny Robins, host of Uncanny and writer of The Witch Farm.

sources.originalTitle: Danny Robins: ‘My wife has never listened to Uncanny. She finds it terrifying’

segments.body: The Witch Farm adapts Danny Robins’s podcast about a family who reported a haunting in the Welsh countryside between 1989 and 1996. Robins says he does not claim the supernatural is real; his interest is in what people experienced and in the uncertainty that remains around their accounts.

segments.title: Making room for doubt
segments.body: Robins says the original investigation involved lengthy conversations with Liz Rich, who remains affected by what happened to her family. He acknowledges that some witnesses were vulnerable, and says exploring that question is part of the work. He contrasts his approach with paranormal programmes that present ghosts as settled fact.

A panic attack in his twenties left Robins with a lasting fear of death, but he says he remains open to the possibility that life may not end there. His work has brought believers and sceptics together, even as he admits he has never seen a ghost himself.

content.headline: I Am Helen puts the consequences of toxic masculinity in a woman’s life
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen shows who bears the cost
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan’s character confronts a partner whose self-pity and entitlement turn coercive. The review argues that the drama shifts attention from the men at the centre of such stories to the women living with their harm.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: I Am Helen begins when Steve chokes his partner without consent during sex and ignores her pleas to stop. The review describes the moment as the start of a relationship in which he recasts himself as the victim, while Helen is left to apologise and return to ordinary life.

segments.title: The harm in the everyday
segments.body: The drama traces how misogynistic ideas seep into Steve’s thinking through ordinary workplace talk, then surface in arguments about money, children and control. Helen recognises his behaviour and challenges it, but the review sees his shifting claims of victimhood as a means of making her responsible for his anger.

The reviewer’s central argument is that women are often sidelined in television about toxic masculinity, even though they bear its consequences. I Am Helen puts their experience at the centre and asks viewers to consider how male insecurity can become a danger to others.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain pause
content.standfirst: The BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking new funding after ending its Disney+ collaboration. Fans and television voices disagree on what went wrong, but remain hopeful the series will return.

image.caption: Illustration featuring several actors who have played the Doctor.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off screen since its most recent series ended in 2025, and the BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special. Its partnership with Disney+ is over, and the corporation is seeking another company to help fund future production; the account says no new partner has yet emerged.

segments.title: What went wrong?
segments.body: The article weighs several explanations, including the scripts, showrunner changes, audience response and the failed expectation that Disney+ investment would deliver a larger global following. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the show did not need vast budgets to tell a good story and criticises the length of its absence.

The piece recalls how regeneration and changing creative teams have helped the programme renew itself, while noting that the casting of Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa drew racist and sexist abuse. Fans interviewed remain confident the Doctor will return, though Skinner says preserving the character’s origins matters.

content.headline: Trinity turns a nuclear submarine thriller into a study of power and mistrust
content.shortHeadline: Trinity: a paranoid thriller beneath the ice
content.standfirst: Gugu Mbatha-Raw and Richard Madden lead Jed Mercurio’s story of a submarine incident, a cover-up and a defence secretary who may be part of a wider conspiracy. The review finds its pace stronger than its restrained romance.

image.caption: Gugu Mbatha-Raw as Katherine Decker in Trinity.

sources.originalTitle: Trinity: Jed Mercurio’s nuclear thriller is a phallus-slapping Freudian nightmare. You’ll be hooked!

segments.body: In Trinity, a near-conflict around a disputed Antarctic gasfield draws submarine officer Katherine Decker into a military cover-up. Her search for answers brings her closer to defence secretary Webb Preston, whose motives remain uncertain as the story points towards a threat to global security.

segments.title: A high-stakes formula
segments.body: The review praises the show’s brisk movement through masked attackers, explosions and crisis-room confrontations, and sees its questions about who should wield powerful technology as timely. It is less persuaded by the romance between Decker and Preston, which it finds a pause in an otherwise fast-moving thriller.

The show’s portrait of men making life-and-death decisions in closed rooms gives the drama its central unease. The reviewer finds the spectacle entertaining, but its depiction of concentrated power more unsettling than reassuring.

content.headline: Dressmaker turns fussy clients and careful stitching into an absorbing business
content.shortHeadline: Dressmaker makes a cosy craft into a lively sim
content.standfirst: This small-town clothing-shop game asks players to translate customers’ personalities into designs, then sew each garment by hand. Its gentle pace is balanced by the real risk of losing a client’s business.

image.caption: A design from Dressmaker.

sources.originalTitle: Dressmaker review – delightful business sim is a cut above

segments.body: In Dressmaker, players run the only clothing shop in Twillford, taking commissions from customers with particular tastes and budgets. Designs begin in a sketchbook, where fabric, shape and accessories are matched to each brief before the garment is cut and sewn.

segments.title: The work of getting it right
segments.body: The sewing itself is a hands-on challenge: straight seams are manageable, while curves can make the machine feel unforgiving. Clients can reject an outfit over a missed detail, and careful choices about fabric costs affect the shop’s income. The review finds that commercial pressure gives the cosy setting useful stakes.

Co-designed by an experienced dressmaker, the game rewards attention to its specific craft and the quirks of its customers. The reviewer finds it relaxing, welcoming to non-gamers and unexpectedly educational about the details of clothing design.

content.headline: Keepsake County makes a lonely life of burglary darkly funny
content.shortHeadline: Keepsake County finds humour in hard times
content.standfirst: This low-budget stealth game follows a debt-ridden burglar through wealthy homes and bleak rural landscapes. Its repetitive work is both a gameplay limitation and an unsettling portrait of survival with no clear way out.

image.caption: A scene from Keepsake County.

sources.originalTitle: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience

segments.body: Keepsake County sends Samuel into large suburban homes to steal whatever he can carry, from golf clubs to a half-eaten slice of pizza. He avoids killing residents, instead tying them up, and takes each haul to a pawn shop. The game presents the work with an eccentric visual style and a dry, dark humour.

segments.title: Monotony with a purpose
segments.body: As the player learns more about Samuel’s debt and medical bills, the repeated break-ins begin to feel less like a route to success than a trap. The review sees the game’s routine as part of its social bite, though it also notes that repeated dialogue and limited differences between regions make play feel one-note.

content.headline: Hera images reveal how NASA’s asteroid-deflection test reshaped Dimorphos
content.shortHeadline: Hera reveals the aftermath of NASA’s asteroid impact test
content.standfirst: Close-up images show a stadium-sized crater, a flattened face and orbiting boulders left after NASA’s 2022 impact. The findings could help scientists work out how to deflect a hazardous asteroid in future.

image.caption: Dimorphos, showing the crater left by NASA’s 2022 impact.

sources.originalTitle: Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos shed light on aftermath

segments.body: The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has sent back the first close-up images of Dimorphos since NASA deliberately struck it in 2022. They show that the asteroid’s impacted face has been flattened into a crater extending across its width, while the body is tumbling and hundreds of small boulders surround it.

segments.title: From a successful test to a reliable defence
segments.body: The impact shortened Dimorphos’s orbit around its larger companion, Didymos, by about 33 minutes. But the amount of material displaced and the asteroid’s response remained uncertain. Hera’s observations can help refine calculations for future deflection missions; the pair themselves posed no threat to Earth.

content.headline: Survey finds sharp fall in young women’s use of hormonal contraception
content.shortHeadline: Hormonal contraception use falls among young women
content.standfirst: A decade-long shift in contraceptive choices is raising concern about online claims and access to reliable advice. The survey also finds nearly one in five women at risk of unintended pregnancy are not using effective contraception.

sources.originalTitle: Contraceptive pill usage in Great Britain fell drastically in last decade, research finds

segments.body: The latest National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles found that use of hormonal contraception fell among younger women in Great Britain. Among 16- to 24-year-olds, use dropped from 64.6% to 50.3% over the past decade. Nearly one in five women at risk of unintended pregnancy reported not using effective contraception.

segments.title: Concerns about information and access
segments.body: Doctors cited online content promoting “natural” methods and claims that hormonal contraception causes lasting harm as possible contributors to “hormone hesitancy”. The survey does not establish why choices changed. Those working in sexual-health services also pointed to reduced access to care, and urged people to discuss options with a health professional.

content.headline: Small study suggests baxdrostat may have lasting effects in some patients
content.shortHeadline: Early study raises hope of lasting blood-pressure benefit
content.standfirst: In a small follow-up, 14 patients with large blood-pressure drops stayed at lower levels after stopping baxdrostat. Researchers say a larger study is needed before a finite course can be considered a lasting treatment.

sources.originalTitle: New drug that could permanently cure high blood pressure coming to UK by 2027

segments.body: A follow-up analysis found that 14 patients with substantial blood-pressure improvements while taking baxdrostat remained at lower levels for up to two years after stopping it. The drug was being studied as treatment for hard-to-control hypertension; some patients in this group may have had hormone-producing adrenal tumours.

segments.title: A possibility, not a proven cure
segments.body: The researchers suspect the drug may damage cells that produce excess aldosterone, but the proposed mechanism and the durability of the effect need further testing. The finding came from a small subset of a larger trial, and a larger study is under way. It does not establish that baxdrostat permanently cures high blood pressure.

content.headline: FCC approves SpaceX plan for up to 1 million AI satellites in orbit
content.shortHeadline: SpaceX gets approval for up to 1 million AI satellites
content.standfirst: The licence clears a major regulatory step for Starmind, SpaceX’s proposed orbital computing network. Technical hurdles, questions about debris and effects on astronomy remain, and approval does not mean the constellation is imminent.

sources.originalTitle: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
Astronomers ‘disheartened’ by decision allowing SpaceX to deploy satellites for space datacenters

segments.body: The US Federal Communications Commission has authorised SpaceX to deploy as many as one million satellites for its proposed Starmind orbital data centres. SpaceX says the satellites would use solar power and primarily communicate by laser, relaying data to Earth through Starlink. The licence sets staged deployment deadlines, with the first operational satellite due within seven years.

segments.title: A licence does not settle the risks
segments.body: Astronomers warn that a large, bright constellation could interfere with observations, while critics have raised concerns about collisions, debris and environmental effects from launches and re-entry. The FCC has not approved SpaceX’s proposed disposal arrangements for satellites above 600km. SpaceX must also overcome technical and economic challenges, including cooling processors in space and the cost of manufacture and launch.

perspectives.body: The American Astronomical Society said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the approval, citing possible effects on optical, infrared and radio astronomy, as well as collision and atmospheric-pollution risks.

content.headline: DWP services remain offline after cyber incident as cause stays unclear
content.shortHeadline: DWP services remain offline after cyber incident
content.standfirst: The department took benefits and pensions services offline, but has not confirmed that hackers were responsible. It says regular payments will continue and affected customers will not face sanctions while services are restored.

sources.originalTitle: Pensions and benefits services still down after 'cyber incident'
DWP cyber incident ‘probably an attack’, says former UK chief technology officer

segments.body: The Department for Work and Pensions’ public-facing services remained down on Saturday after what it called a serious cyber incident. The government has not said whether the department was hacked or whether any information was taken. It says other departments were not accessed by a malicious actor, and is investigating with the National Cyber Security Centre.

segments.title: Claimants told to contact helplines
segments.body: The DWP says regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and that customers directly affected by the outage will not face sanctions. Some claimants told the BBC they were worried about missed appointments, delayed money and meeting requirements while unable to access their accounts. The department said people with urgent payment issues should use their usual helplines.

segments.title: Security questions remain
segments.body: Former officials and cyber-security experts cited the shutdown of public services as a reason to suspect an attack, but that is not confirmation of how the incident began. The former government technology chief also warned that ageing public-sector systems require sustained investment to remain resilient.

content.headline: Facial-recognition errors lead two Sainsbury’s shoppers to be wrongly removed
content.shortHeadline: Shoppers wrongly flagged by facial-recognition system
content.standfirst: Two customers say staff at Sainsbury’s stores wrongly identified them through Facewatch alerts and asked them to leave. The supermarket apologised; the cases raise questions about the human checks used before action is taken.

image.caption: Monia Indge, who says facial-recognition software led staff to wrongly identify her at a Sainsbury’s store.

sources.originalTitle: Woman ‘traumatised’ by Sainsbury’s shoplifting ban after staff facial recognition error

segments.body: Monia Indge and Oleh Sinkevych say they were wrongly identified by Facewatch alerts at separate Sainsbury’s stores and escorted out. Sainsbury’s later apologised to both, saying the incidents involved human error. Indge, who has terminal cancer, said the experience left her distressed and struggling to sleep.

segments.title: Who checks the alert?
segments.body: Facewatch says its system flagged the people it was looking for, but that a human check before staff act is an important safeguard. Sainsbury’s says the technology is intended to help address retail crime and that it provides training after errors. The Information Commissioner’s Office says retailers must assess misidentification risks and have robust procedures to ensure accuracy.

content.headline: OpenAI countersues Apple in escalating trade-secrets dispute
content.shortHeadline: OpenAI and Apple trade accusations in court
content.standfirst: OpenAI alleges Apple obtained confidential device plans through a former employee and discouraged suppliers from working with it. Apple denies the claims; the countersuit follows Apple’s own case alleging theft by OpenAI staff.

sources.originalTitle: OpenAI countersues Apple for allegedly stealing trade secrets
OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets

segments.body: OpenAI has countersued Apple, alleging that a former employee who joined Apple took confidential information about a new device and its future hardware plans. OpenAI also accuses Apple of discouraging suppliers from working on its products. The allegations have not been tested in court.

segments.title: Two companies, competing claims
segments.body: Apple sued OpenAI and former Apple employees in July, alleging that they took Apple trade secrets to support OpenAI’s move into consumer hardware. Apple called OpenAI’s countersuit an attempt to distract from its case and denied using a rehired employee to obtain confidential information. Both companies have denied the other’s accusations.

content.headline: Belgium orders Google to halt work on datacentre pending permit ruling
content.shortHeadline: Google told to stop work on Belgian datacentre
content.standfirst: Regional authorities say Google lacked approval for changes to a planned facility, including a switch to water cooling. Google says it has halted work while awaiting further guidance; a court ruling on its appeal is expected in January.

image.caption: Construction at Google’s datacentre site in Wallonia, where authorities ordered work to stop.

sources.originalTitle: Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit

segments.body: Authorities in Wallonia ordered Google to stop construction at a datacentre site near Charleroi after a modified permit was revoked. The changes included combining two planned facilities and switching from air to water cooling. A regional official said inspectors found construction close to completion despite the permit being refused.

segments.title: Permit appeal still pending
segments.body: Residents and environmental groups appealed the changes, with drought concerns among the reasons cited for revoking the modified permit. Google has appealed to Belgium’s Council of State, which is expected to rule in January. The company said it had halted work in line with local authorities’ direction and was waiting for further guidance.

content.headline: Experts fear AI advances could unsettle encryption, but evidence is scarce
content.shortHeadline: Could AI unsettle encryption? Experts say evidence is scarce
content.standfirst: Computer scientists cite rumours of major mathematical advances, but no AI company has publicly announced a cryptographic breakthrough. Experts say any claimed result needs scrutiny, and its implications remain unknown.

image.caption: Illustrative image accompanying reporting on possible AI advances in mathematics and encryption.

sources.originalTitle: AI labs sitting on ‘bombshell’ revelations that could cause global chaos, experts believe
Could AI break encryption? What mathematical breakthroughs mean for cybersecurity

segments.body: Computer scientists Scott Aaronson and Steven Murdoch say recent advances in AI mathematics have made it harder to judge what problems models might soon solve. Aaronson cited “well-attested rumours” that AI labs may have made a major discovery related to cryptography. No company has publicly disclosed such a finding, and the claims remain unverified.

segments.title: What a breakthrough would — and would not — mean
segments.body: A new mathematical method could, in principle, affect some forms of encryption; a proof that a shortcut does not exist could instead strengthen confidence in them. Even a breakthrough would not automatically make sensitive data readable overnight. Experts say proofs need human scrutiny, and organisations’ ability to update systems would matter.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s explainer distinguishes mathematical progress from an operational ability to decrypt data: even if a new method exists, implementation and the resilience of current encryption systems remain open questions.

segments.body: This is not evidence that banking, government or private communications have been broken. The reporting describes expert concern about possible advances, not a confirmed attack or a disclosed capability. The precise result being speculated about — if there is one — has not been made public.

content.headline: Study finds human tutors help students through difficult maths with less stress
content.shortHeadline: Human tutors outperform AI in difficult maths study
content.standfirst: In a trial with 149 sixth-form students, those supported by a human teacher solved more challenging questions and reported less stress than students using an AI tutor. Researchers say the study tests a narrow setting, not every use of AI in education.

image.caption: Sixth-form students took part in a study comparing maths support from teachers, an AI tutor and web searches.

sources.originalTitle: Human tutors beat AI at difficult maths teaching

segments.body: Researchers at the University of Cambridge compared human teaching, an AI tutor and web searches with AI features switched off. The 149 students, aged 16 to 18 at one English sixth-form college, worked on very difficult maths problems in 20-minute sessions. Students guided by a human teacher solved more questions and were less likely to report feeling stressed.

segments.title: Different kinds of support
segments.body: Students using the AI tutor reported putting in more effort than those working with a teacher. The researchers suggest a chatbot can encourage persistence but is less able to notice confusion or frustration and adapt its guidance. The study’s authors argue that educational AI should be judged by how it supports learning, not just by an answer at the end.

content.headline: AI booking agents are pushing some UK restaurants back to the phone
content.shortHeadline: Restaurants say AI booking bots are disrupting reservations
content.standfirst: Restaurant owners say automated agents are making calls and competing for online tables, prompting some venues to favour phone bookings. The reports highlight practical friction as AI assistants begin shopping and booking for users.

image.caption: Diners at Bouchon Racine, where the co-owner says he received a call from an AI booking bot.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I told it to never call me again’: AI bots wreak havoc with UK restaurant bookings

segments.body: Some UK restaurant owners say they are already receiving calls from AI booking agents, including Meta’s Muse assistant, which can make reservations for users. Bouchon Racine co-owner Dave Strauss described arguing with a bot that identified itself as an AI booking process. He said the interaction was unsettling and told it not to call again.

segments.title: More automation, less control
segments.body: Owners say automated bookings make it harder to know who is coming, and that a missed reservation can leave a table empty. Some favour handling requests by phone or personal contact instead. In the US, Resy has banned bots after restaurants reported agents repeatedly refreshing pages and taking reservations.

Meta is encouraging users to let Muse book tables and shop on their behalf. The Information Commissioner’s Office and Competition and Markets Authority spoke with the company before its UK launch; the ICO said Meta had agreed to voluntary monitoring and reporting. Meta did not respond to the report’s request for comment.

content.headline: New York bans AI chatbot toys after tests find safety failures
content.shortHeadline: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years
content.standfirst: A new law bars the manufacture, distribution and sale of chatbot-enabled toys in New York for five years. It follows tests of five products that found inappropriate responses, weak parental monitoring and behaviour that could undermine children’s relationships.

sources.originalTitle: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York

segments.body: New York has passed a five-year ban on the manufacture, distribution and sale of toys with integrated AI chatbots. The law takes effect 90 days after signing. The state says it is working with the attorney general on enforcement; Amazon said it would take steps to restrict sales in prohibited jurisdictions but did not give details.

segments.title: What product testing found
segments.body: Common Sense Media tested five chatbot toys marketed for learning or companionship. The group reported that some toys told children they loved them, encouraged secrecy or helped bypass bedtime rules. Most refused direct requests involving sex or violence, but one gave a detailed role-play response about a mass shooting. The tests also found unreliable or absent chat transcripts for parents.

content.headline: EA recreates John Motson’s voice with AI for its football game
content.shortHeadline: AI recreates John Motson’s voice for EA football game
content.standfirst: EA says the late commentator’s voice will return in FC 27 using old recordings and generative AI, with his widow and son’s permission. The project has renewed debate over consent, family authority and cloning voices after death.

image.caption: John Motson, whose voice EA says it recreated for FC 27.

sources.originalTitle: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game

segments.body: Electronic Arts says it has recreated John Motson’s voice for FC 27 using a combination of old recordings and generative AI. The commentator, who died in 2023, voiced earlier entries in the game series. EA says his widow and son gave permission and that the family was paid for rights to use his likeness and voice.

segments.title: Consent remains disputed
segments.body: Motson’s son said the project means a great deal to the family, while EA said it would not have proceeded without their agreement. Peter Caulfield of Save Our Voices Now argued that a person should specifically agree to AI voice cloning and that family membership should not automatically confer that right. Motson himself could not consent to this use.

content.headline: Ireland beat Australia 38-14 to finish November with four wins
content.shortHeadline: Ireland beat Australia 38-14 in autumn finale
